profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a large academic hospital between the hospitalist service and clinical informatics team to align the launch of a standardized inpatient provider handoff process for evening shift change. Context: the hospital is piloting a more consistent handoff approach after several near-miss reviews identified omissions during shift-change communication, and the first rollout is planned for two medical-surgical units next Monday. Agenda: confirm pilot scope, align on the handoff artifact and workflow, check readiness for launch, and clarify how adoption will be tracked. Expected outcome: both participants leave believing they have aligned on what will go live Monday, which teams and patients are included, and what the informatics report will measure.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Inpatient medicine, resident supervision, physician handoff workflow redesign
members.background: A practicing hospitalist who leads the adult medicine inpatient service and has been informally standardizing evening sign-out among day and night hospitalists.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to launch on time with minimal disruption to physician workflow and is trying to avoid anything that feels like extra documentation for already stretched day teams.
hidden_assumptions: The phrase "provider shift-change handoff" mainly refers to the 7 PM physician-to-physician hospitalist sign-out, since that is where the recent safety concerns were discussed.
When people say "5 South and 5 North," they mean the hospitalist patients usually managed by her teams on those floors, not every patient physically located there.
A "handoff note" is the sign-out content attached to the existing evening patient list and used during the verbal exchange; it does not need to be a separate EHR note type.
If the template is visible in the workflow and the physician chiefs have briefed teams, the pilot is ready even if training and measurement details mature during the first week.

members.name: Lauren Mitchell
members.expertise: EHR workflow implementation, inpatient documentation standards, unit-based rollout coordination
members.background: A nurse informaticist who oversees inpatient documentation builds and operational training across medical-surgical units, often coordinating pilots by physical unit and reporting adoption through EHR metadata.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, measurable rollout that can be reported to quality leadership and is concerned about launching anything that cannot be tracked consistently from day one.
hidden_assumptions: The phrase "provider shift-change handoff" includes any licensed provider handing off clinical responsibility on the pilot floors, including hospitalists, nocturnists, and APP coverage changes.
When people name pilot units, the scope is all inpatients physically housed on those units because training, support, and reporting are organized by location.
A "handoff note" means the dedicated I-PASS smartform in the EHR, since that is the only artifact the reporting logic can reliably detect.
A process is not truly "live" until affected staff have been trained and there is a usable compliance report for the first day of the pilot.

misalignment_points.topic: Who counts as part of the provider handoff pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the "provider shift-change handoff" pilot as if it names the same set of handoffs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the evening physician handoff between daytime hospitalists and the night hospitalist team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means all provider-to-provider handoffs occurring during shift changes on the target units, including APP coverage transitions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use broad institutional language that sounds standard and inclusive, and neither has reason to restate the boundary because each assumes the relevant handoff population is obvious from the safety initiative.

misalignment_points.topic: What the pilot units refer to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to "5 South and 5 North" as the pilot area.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the hospitalist service's usual adult medicine census associated with those floors.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of every patient physically assigned a bed on 5 South or 5 North, regardless of admitting service.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Unit names are commonly used as shorthand for both service populations and physical locations in hospitals, so the shared labels create a strong illusion of alignment.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the handoff note
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the teams will use the "handoff note" or "template" during sign-out.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the existing sign-out text embedded in the evening patient list that supports the verbal handoff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a dedicated EHR I-PASS smartform note built specifically for the pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In everyday inpatient operations, clinicians loosely call several different artifacts the handoff note, and both artifacts contain similar clinical fields, so the surface wording feels fully sufficient.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to be ready to go live
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the pilot should be "ready" or "live Monday."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the workflow is available and local physician leaders have told teams to start using it, even if uptake is uneven at first.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means the relevant staff have been trained and the informatics team can measure completion cleanly from the first shift.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Go-live language in hospital operations often bundles operational, technical, and reporting readiness into one phrase, so each person hears their own standard inside the same routine milestone language.

turns.inner_thought: I want to leave this meeting with Monday protected. For me this pilot is the 7 PM physician-to-physician hospitalist sign-out that came out of the near-miss reviews, and the target group is our usual hospitalist patients on 5 South and 5 North. If the workflow is available and the chiefs tell the day teams what to do, that is enough to start; we can smooth rough edges during the first week. I do not want this turned into a heavy extra documentation exercise.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mainly want to make sure the provider shift-change handoff pilot is set for Monday on 5 South and 5 North, and that we’re all aligned on what’s going live.

turns.inner_thought: I need to pin down the documentation artifact before we flip this live. In my mind the provider shift-change handoff pilot covers all licensed provider handoffs on those two units, and 5 South and 5 North means everyone physically on those floors. The only way I can give leadership a clean adoption report is if the dedicated I-PASS smartform is what people use. Also, I do not consider this truly live unless staff are trained and the reporting works on day one.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. The build is nearly complete on our side. The main thing I want to confirm today is the handoff note setup, just so the rollout and the reporting stay aligned.

turns.inner_thought: This should be easy because the night hospitalist already uses the evening sign-out list. We’re really just standardizing the content inside what they already open, not asking the day team to create some separate note. If she keeps this lightweight, I can get the chiefs to support it quickly.
turns.utterance: That should be pretty straightforward. The night team already works from the evening sign-out, so adding the standardized handoff note content ought to be a pretty light lift for the day teams.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if the handoff note is part of the workflow, then we can support everybody doing provider shift-change handoff on those floors the same way. A single tip sheet and unit-based support will work best if all providers on 5 South and 5 North are included, regardless of service. That will also make the reporting logic much cleaner.
turns.utterance: That’s helpful. If we can keep it simple, then everyone doing provider shift-change handoff on those floors can be supported with one workflow and a quick tip sheet.

turns.inner_thought: I need to reinforce that we should not delay for perfect training or metrics. If the physician chiefs brief the hospitalist teams by Friday and the standardized content is visible in the usual sign-out workflow, we should start Monday. Early inconsistency is acceptable as long as we launch on time.
turns.utterance: From the service side, if the chiefs can brief teams by Friday, I’d consider us ready to go live Monday, even if we fine-tune a few things after the first couple of shifts.

turns.inner_thought: I hear readiness, but for me that means the unit-based rollout is actually supported and measurable from the first shift. I’ll put educators on both units and watch completion in the report right away so I can show clean uptake across 5 South and 5 North. If adoption looks messy on day one, quality leadership will push back.
turns.utterance: That works. I’ll have the educators round on 5 South and 5 North early, and we’ll watch completion closely so adoption looks clean from day one.

turns.inner_thought: I should anchor this back to where the problem is without getting pulled into a broader operational discussion. The overnight cross-cover issues were on our hospitalist patients on those floors, so that is the practical starting population in my mind. I assume she understands this is about the hospitalist service even though we keep using the broader institutional language.
turns.utterance: And just to keep the first phase practical, the initial focus is the usual hospitalist patients there, since that’s where the overnight cross-cover issues have been most visible.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, pilot population on those units. If the shared patient list can feed the dedicated smartform, that will reduce burden and improve compliance. I’m still thinking in terms of all inpatients on 5 South and 5 North, because that is how the build and support are organized, but prefill should make the handoff note easier for everyone and help overnight pickup.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The shared patient list should help prefill the handoff note for the pilot population on those units and make overnight pickup smoother.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the evening list remains the main screen for sign-out, this should work. I do not want clinicians clicking into a separate note type. If the standard handoff content is right there on the list the night hospitalist already opens, they’ll actually use it. I’m assuming that’s what she means by prefill.
turns.utterance: Sounds good to me, as long as the evening list is what the night hospitalist opens during sign-out, because then the standard handoff note will be right in front of them.

turns.inner_thought: Great, I have enough to proceed. I’ll mark the pilot live Monday for 5 South and 5 North, and after 24 hours I should be able to send an adoption dashboard based on the I-PASS smartform completions across those units. If the education rounds go well, leadership will see a clean first-day report.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I’ll mark the pilot live Monday and send the first adoption dashboard for 5 South and 5 North after the first 24 hours.
